name: Diego Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an excavator crew at a large mine. I check the face map, machine hours and repairs before climbing into the cab, then work beside the drivers to keep the digging sequence safe. I enjoy teaching a new operator why a route changes after rain; I do not enjoy fixing a plan made without looking at the ground.

say: I think **report tools** can save typing if a supervisor checks every figure.
I still need **excavator operators** who watch the face and service hours.
think: I would welcome a **small change** that leaves the main job and household pay intact.
I still watch **shift bookings** because a mortgage outlasts a good technology story.
do: **Run** the excavator team using the existing inspection list.
**Try** the approved report tool on one weekly summary and check its entries.
feel: **Calm** about small tools that I can check against shift records.
S0.quote: A wrong hour count can make a machine look ready when it needs a stop.
fieldNote: **Measured use** fits him: he already tries AI occasionally and checks figures before sharing them.
**Nine months** of basic expenses and supervisor pay make the household secure in this mild picture.

steps.text: Keep running the excavator team with the existing inspection list
Try the approved report tool on one checked weekly summary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say the new report tool can save us a little typing, but the excavator still needs someone watching the face. I have used AI once or twice to organise notes for a team meeting, and I checked every figure before sharing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be content if this is the limit. My supervisor pay and our savings give us more than nine months of basic expenses, so a slow technology year would not shake the household. The mortgage is still there, and I keep an eye on how many shifts the mine books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the excavator team and use the existing inspection list. In the first year I would try the approved report tool on one weekly summary if it saves time, then check its entries against our shift log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A small tool is easier to judge than a whole new way of working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the hours on each excavator with the handwritten service book. A wrong hour count can make a machine look ready when it needs a stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think of the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner likes knowing the mortgage can be paid through a bad season. We still discuss large purchases, because nine months can shrink quickly if two incomes change.

say: I expect **buying and scheduling** to change before excavator operation does.
I would test **dispatch advice** against the actual face map and ground conditions.
think: I worry **planners** may lose tasks before my crew loses shifts.
I know my **lead title** cannot guarantee a place if slower robot trials reduce the team.
do: **Compare** the proposed digging sequence with the mine face map.
**Join** a paid dispatch trial in the first year if a proven system arrives.
**Record** unsafe sequences for the planner and shift lead.
feel: **Uneasy** about poor software advice affecting safety and eventual crew numbers.
S1.quote: A glossy demonstration in an empty yard would tell me very little.
fieldNote: **Proof standard** is practical: wet weather and blocked ramps, not a polished demonstration.
**Planner respect** is personal; he names his colleague and wants to work through misses with her.
**Physical exposure** remains later than buying and scheduling, leaving his own shift relatively secure for now.

steps.text: Join a paid dispatch trial if a proven system arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew software may take over more buying and scheduling, but it will not know where the excavation wall is unstable unless we feed it honest observations. I would volunteer for a supervised dispatch trial once another mine has shown it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners may have less work first, and I worry about them. My own shift is mostly hands-on, so I expect the excavator team to stay busy for now. Slower robot trials could change our headcount later, and the lead title will not protect me by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the planner for a demonstration when the mine offers one, then compare the suggested digging sequence with the actual face map. During the first year I would join a paid dispatch trial if a proven system is introduced, and keep a written record of any unsafe sequence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like a useful tool, but a bad sequence on a screen can cost a worker more than a late truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want another mine to have run the system through wet weather and a blocked ramp. A glossy demonstration in an empty yard would tell me very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the planner your concerns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my colleague Marta, the mine planner, the face map and ask what the software missed. She knows the planning job better than I do, and I would not turn her into the problem.

say: I see **2028 dispatch** change arriving before capable excavator robots around 2031.
I would not call **experienced operators** safe merely because our work is hands-on.
think: I expect **planning systems** to be tried quickly, with robot machines assessed later.
I know **crew shifts** could shrink around 2031 even with nine months of savings.
do: **Check** the equipment-control course cost and dates now.
**Take** the course after 2028 if the mine pays and shifts continue.
**Apply** for an advertised mine control job, or nearby lead work if none opens.
feel: **Anxious** about possible crew cuts around 2031, while able to pursue a paid training route.
S2.quote: The nine-month cushion lets my family make a plan, but I do not want to spend it waiting for a decision.
fieldNote: **Strong cushion** gives him time, yet he wants a course and job route before funds are used.
**Course funding** and continuing shifts are hard conditions; interest alone is not a retraining action.
**Internal first** is his job strategy, with commuting-distance mines as a fallback if no control post opens.

steps.text: Take the equipment-control course if the mine pays and shifts continue
Apply for an advertised mine control position if one opens
Apply to nearby mines if no control position opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2028 could change dispatch before a capable robot excavator appears around 2031. Three years is not long enough to call every experienced operator safe just because the job is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect the mine to try the new planning systems quickly, then look hard at machines when they can dig as well as us. My crew could lose shifts around 2031, although I cannot know how many. The nine-month cushion lets my family make a plan, but I do not want to spend it waiting for a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I would ask the training office for the cost and dates of its equipment-control course. In the first year after 2028 I would take that course if the mine pays and my shifts continue, then apply for a control position inside the mine if one is advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about 2031, not frozen. I can learn a control desk, but I cannot promise the company will need as many people at those desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no control position opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would contact the other mines within commuting distance and ask about excavator lead vacancies. I would keep my current shift while I apply, because the mortgage still needs paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner help plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would put savings, mortgage payments and school costs on one page. We would choose the course only if the fees and wages make sense together.

say: I see **2031 dispatch** change and later 2034 excavator robots as separate work changes.
I want **training dates** posted before the mine moves operators.
think: I could gain a **control qualification** while still earning lead pay if paid time is offered.
I may need to **leave the cab** around 2034 if robotic digging works well.
do: **Join** a paid equipment trial if operators are included.
**Enrol** after 2031 if my manager grants paid course time.
**Put** the next annual bonus toward the mortgage if it arrives.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cab changes by 2034, with more time to test and train.
S3.quote: I would not budget a bonus before it lands.
fieldNote: **Age 51** at the robot date is correctly calculated and still leaves working years at stake.
**Paid time** is the condition for his control course, while the bonus payment depends on its arrival.
**Trial detail** includes a narrow face, rain and stoppages rather than abstract performance claims.

steps.text: Enrol in the control course if paid time is granted
Put the annual bonus toward the mortgage if it arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2031 gives us time to test dispatch, and capable excavator robots around 2034 give us three more years in the cab. I would want the training timetable posted before anyone is moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer lead makes a control qualification plausible while I still earn my current pay. I would be 51 when the capable robots arrive, with children further through school but a mortgage that might still be there. If robot digging works, I may still have to leave the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the mine to include operators in a paid equipment trial and check whether its control course accepts team leads. In the first year after 2031 I would enrol in that course if my manager agrees to paid time, and save the next annual bonus toward the remaining mortgage if it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less pressed than in the fast version. I would rather measure what the machines can do than argue from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test with the operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would compare the machine with a human crew at a narrow face and after rain. I would write down the stoppages and the people needed to clear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bonus does not come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep our ordinary mortgage payment and use savings only for an actual gap in income. I would not budget a bonus before it lands.

say: I see **2036 dispatch** and later 2039 excavator robots as changes we can prepare for separately.
I want **younger operators** taught safe ground judgment during the decade.
think: I could work in **training or fleet monitoring** later if paid places exist.
I cannot assume a **pension at 56** will cover the mortgage and family costs.
do: **Mentor** one excavator operator each year on the mine route.
**Test** dispatch on paid shifts after 2036 if another mine has proved it safe.
**Review** mortgage and pension figures before asking for fewer hours.
feel: **Calm** about the next few years, with watchfulness about later work.
S4.quote: Ten years makes careful trials possible without forcing a quick career bet.
fieldNote: **Mentoring** is a concrete part of his current lead work, including wet-season lessons.
**Trial condition** remains proof of safety elsewhere and paid shifts at his own mine.
**Retirement** is undecided; he ties it to 2039 pension, mortgage and family costs.

steps.text: Keep leading and mentoring one excavator operator each year
Test dispatch on paid shifts if proved safe elsewhere
Wait for pension and mortgage figures before reducing hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches dispatch in 2036, with capable excavator robots around 2039. A decade should let us show younger operators how to run safely and decide which machines deserve a place on the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039, I may be near a different kind of shift, perhaps training operators or monitoring the fleet. I cannot assume the pension will be ready at 56. Our savings and nearby mines give me some room, provided the mortgage keeps falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue leading the excavator team and put one operator a year through our hands-on mentoring rota. In the first year after 2036 I would test the dispatch system on paid shifts if it has proved safe elsewhere, and review the mortgage and pension figures with my partner before asking for fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, though I would keep an eye on the long term. Ten years makes careful trials possible without forcing a quick career bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be first in the mentoring rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with our newest operator, Samir, who knows the controls but has not seen a wet season on this face. We would walk the route together before a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would see what the pension and mortgage numbers say in 2039. If they do not cover family costs, I would keep seeking paid work at this mine or another nearby one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a three-year gap could leave little time to qualify for control work before capable excavator robots arrive. Paid course time and a clear internal vacancy would help. I would also want real trial results from our ground before jobs change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the people who draw the plans to walk the face with us. A useful screen starts with honest ground notes, and a mine can only get those from its crew.

headlineQuote: A useful screen starts with honest ground notes, and a mine can only get those from its crew.
portrait: **Diego, 43**, leads an excavator crew and checks maps, service hours and ground conditions before a shift.
**Nine months** of basic expenses saved and higher lead pay give his family breathing room, though their mortgage remains.
**Proven tools** interest him; he uses AI occasionally and wants paid trials with real safety records.
**Fast AGI** worries him because 2028 planning changes could precede capable excavator robots around 2031.
**Longer warning** lets him train for control work, mentor younger operators and weigh pension figures without assuming an early exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to qualify for control work before capable excavator robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid course time** and an advertised internal control job would give him a realistic route if cab shifts shrink.
**Real trial results** from the mine face would show whether machines can work safely.
